Find the Right Tool

"Camera test" and "webcam test" usually mean the same thing — pick what you're actually checking below

Both phrases almost always describe the same basic need: confirming a camera works and previewing its live feed. "Webcam" traditionally implied a separate USB device plugged into a desktop, while "camera" is more often used for a laptop's built-in camera or a phone — but in practice the two terms are used interchangeably, and every tool on this site works the same regardless of which type of camera you have.

content_html:
Ever wondered whether your camera test vs webcam test explained distinction actually matters when you're preparing for a critical job interview or client presentation? Whether you call it a check camera or a test webcam, what counts is knowing — with certainty — that your video feed is clear, your frame rate is smooth, and your data stays protected. This page gives you that certainty: a free, instant, browser-based online webcam testing tool that runs entirely on your device, surfaces every key metric in seconds, and helps you walk into your next call looking polished and professional.

What Is a Webcam Test and Why Does It Matter — Camera Test vs Webcam Test Explained

A webcam tester is a diagnostic tool that activates your computer camera through the browser, renders a live feed, and reports technical data about your device — all without installing any application. Unlike a general diagnostic performed inside a native app, a browser-based checker works the same way that video call platforms and meeting tools do: it requests browser permission through the browser's media API. That makes it the most realistic pre-call diagnostic available.

The practical difference matters for remote work, online meetings, live broadcast, and content creation. If your camera works in the operating system's camera utility but fails in your web client, you have an access rights problem — not a device problem. Running a quick webcam check in the same client you use for online conferencing catches that mismatch before your audience does.

How a Browser-Based Camera Test Works — Frame Rate and Feed Detection

When you load this page, the webcam tester invokes the browser's getUserMedia API — a standard interface supported by Google Chrome, a popular open-source web client, Safari, and Microsoft Edge on both desktop and handheld devices. The client issues a browser prompt asking whether to allow camera access. Once you click Allow, the stream is rendered locally; every frame is locally processed and never transmitted anywhere. This is what client side testing means: your image stays on your machine.

The tool simultaneously reads device details — image dimensions, capture rate capabilities, display proportions, sensor resolution, device label, and audio device presence — and displays them in the Camera Information panel. No upload, no capture stored on a server, no footage shared with anyone. Everything is locally in browser, giving you complete data protection and instant diagnostics.

Compatible devices include PCs running Microsoft Windows 11, MacBooks running the Apple operating system, desktop machines running open-source OS environments (where tools like the Cheese app and cameractrls are common alternatives), Android phones, iPhones running the mobile web client, tablets, and Chromebooks. Essentially any device with a modern web environment and a camera — whether a built-in laptop webcam, an external webcam plugged into a connector port, or a phone camera — works with this tool.

What the 30-Second Webcam Check Verifies in One Pass

A good 30-second webcam check confirms more than you might expect. Here is what the tester evaluates in a single session:

  • Live feed presence — confirms the camera is connected and working and that a visual output is being produced
  • Resolution — the highest resolution the device is currently outputting, from 480p through 4K
  • Frame rate (FPS) — real, measured fps delivered to the client, not the manufacturer's claimed maximum
  • Aspect ratio — whether the feed is 16:9, 4:3, or another ratio that could cause image stretch or letterboxed output
  • Webcam megapixels — calculated from the active resolution to indicate sensor capability
  • Camera facing — front-facing (selfie), rear-facing, or external
  • Built-in microphone presence — confirms your mic is recognised alongside the camera, which is useful when you also need to test microphone functionality
  • Built-in speaker presence — detects whether an audio output device is linked to the webcam
  • PNG file size and JPEG file size — still-image compression benchmarks that indicate sensor colour richness
  • Number of colors — a colour depth indicator reflecting the camera's imaging capability

All of this happens automatically once you grant permission. There is no manual configuration, no installation needed, no account creation, and no application required.

How to Run a Check Camera Online on Any Device — Windows, Mac, and Linux

Before you run the browser-based test webcam online, it is worth verifying that your operating system recognises the camera at all. OS-level diagnostics establish a baseline: if the camera works in native applications but fails in the web client, the fault is in web client permissions or a conflicting program. If it fails at the OS level, the issue is in device drivers, the physical component, or system configuration.

Running a Webcam Test on Windows — Settings and Privacy Access

Windows provides a built-in path to confirm camera access before any web client is involved:

  1. Open Settings (Win + I) and navigate to Privacy & Security → Camera.
  2. Confirm that Camera access is toggled On at the device level under the system's data-protection controls.
  3. Scroll down and ensure that desktop applications and the web client you use are individually permitted — this is the configuration layer that governs which apps access camera resources.
  4. Open the Windows Camera app from the Start menu. If your feed appears, the OS is correctly recognising the device. Watch for flicker, lag, or a black screen.
  5. If no feed appears, open the hardware manager utility, expand Cameras or Imaging Devices, and check for warning icons that signal driver issues.
  6. Right-click the camera entry and choose Update driver to refresh the device software from the manufacturer's website if needed.

Problems at this stage — camera disabled, permission denied, or missing device software — must be resolved before the browser-based tool will show a feed. Once the Windows Camera app displays a clean image, your camera functions at the OS level and you can move to the web client step.

Running a Camera Test on Mac or Linux — System Preferences and Security

On macOS, System Preferences (or System Settings on macOS Ventura and later) governs camera access at the OS level. Follow these steps:

  1. Open System Preferences → Security & Privacy → Camera (this is the macOS camera configuration panel).
  2. Check that your web client — whether the Apple browser, a Chromium-based client, or an open-source alternative — appears in the list and has camera access enabled. This is your baseline confirmation.
  3. Open Photo Booth as a quick native camera check. If your feed appears there, the device and OS are communicating correctly.
  4. If you are using an iPhone as a webcam (available on macOS Ventura+), verify it appears as an option in the camera selection dropdown in supported apps.

On open-source desktop systems, open the Cheese app and navigate to Preferences to select your device. Use the OS camera access controls — typically found in Settings → Privacy → Camera — to confirm access is permitted. If cameractrls is installed, it provides granular per-device controls for connected camera devices. Missing device software on these platforms is addressed by checking lsusb output and installing the relevant kernel modules from the manufacturer website.

How to Check Camera Online Directly in a Browser — Granting Camera Access

Once the OS recognises your camera, the browser-based webcam tester is the fastest way to check camera online and verify working status under real conferencing conditions. The steps are identical regardless of platform:

  • Open this page in Google Chrome, an open-source web client, the Apple browser, or Edge on desktop or handheld devices.
  • Click the Start button (also called the test button) at the top of the tool widget.
  • A browser prompt will appear: click Allow to grant camera access and, optionally, sound input rights to test microphone noise levels.
  • Your camera preview appears instantly. The Camera Information panel populates with your device label, resolution, and other metrics.
  • If you have multiple cameras, use the device selector or camera dropdown to switch cameras and test each one in turn.

On the Apple mobile browser and Android's web client, the same prompt appears. Grant access and the live preview renders your smartphone camera feed. This is particularly useful if you intend to use your phone as a webcam during a meeting. Accessibility is a core design goal — the tool works across all mainstream platforms and mobile environments.

To grant or revoke rights after the initial prompt, navigate to your web client's page-level controls: in the Chromium-based client, open Settings → Privacy and Security → Site Settings → Camera; in the Apple browser, open the OS preferences → Security and Privacy → Camera; in the open-source web client, click the lock icon in the address bar and adjust camera rights per site.

Understanding Your Online Webcam Test Results — Camera Information Explained

Once your feed is live, the Camera Information panel is where the real value lies. Each field tells you something specific about your camera's performance and device capabilities. Understanding these metrics lets you make informed decisions about whether your configuration meets the demands of professional video call sessions, live broadcast, capturing footage, or online class participation.

Breaking Down Every Camera Information Field — Image Quality and Resolution

Field Name What It Tells You
Webcam Name: The label and model of the webcam as reported to the web client. Useful for device comparison, identifying which physical unit is active, and searching for the correct device software.
Frame Rate: The actual real fps being delivered to the web client right now — not the advertised maximum. 30 fps is the standard for professional online meetings; 60 fps benefits broadcast and capture work. Below 15 fps produces choppy and delayed footage that feels unprofessional.
Webcam Resolution: The active pixel dimensions (e.g., 1920×1080 for Full HD). Higher resolution means greater sharpness and detail. 720p (1280×720) is the minimum acceptable for business calls; 1080p is the professional standard. This is your maximum output under current web client configuration.
Aspect Ratio: The width-to-height ratio of the stream. Standard widescreen is 16:9. An unexpected ratio (e.g., 4:3) can cause your image to appear letterboxed or stretched inside meeting platforms — particularly important for device comparison across setups.
Webcam Megapixels: Calculated from resolution width × height ÷ 1,000,000. Higher sensor resolution generally corresponds to richer detail and larger still captures. A 1080p camera delivers approximately 2.1 MP; a 4K camera delivers roughly 8.3 MP.
Camera Facing: Indicates whether the camera is front-facing (typical for laptop built-in cameras and phones in selfie mode), rear-facing, or environment-facing. Relevant when using a smartphone camera as a webcam or toggling between lenses.
Built-in Microphone: Confirms whether a sound input device is linked to the webcam. Many external webcams include an integrated mic; knowing whether yours does helps you decide whether to route audio from the webcam or from a separate sound interface.
Built-in Speaker: Shows whether a sound output device is associated with your webcam. Useful when diagnosing sound routing on meeting platforms.
PNG File Size: The file size of a lossless still captured from the live stream. Larger PNG sizes indicate richer colour depth and more detail per frame — relevant to real-world image assessments.
JPEG File Size: The compressed still size. A healthy ratio between PNG and JPEG sizes suggests good colour accuracy and minimal banding. Very small JPEG sizes can indicate low bit depth or aggressive web client compression.
Number of Colors: A pixel-sampled colour count from the live frame, reflecting the camera's ability to reproduce accurate hue and saturation. Higher counts suggest better colour balance and richness — important for professional-looking footage.

Interpreting Good vs. Poor Values — FPS, Aspect Ratio, and Image Quality Standards

Knowing the numbers is only useful if you understand what they mean in practice. Here is a quick reference for evaluating your results:

  • Frame rate (FPS): 30 fps or above is the target for professional online meetings. 60 fps is preferred for live broadcast and screen capture work. Anything below 15 fps produces visible motion blur and freeze artefacts. The capture rate supported by the device may be higher than what the web client reports under heavy CPU load — close unused tabs to improve throughput.
  • Resolution: 1080p (1920×1080) is the professional standard. 720p is acceptable for internal team sessions. 480p or lower produces blurry results and is a sign that supported dimensions are being limited by device software or web client access settings.
  • Aspect ratio: 16:9 is correct for most modern webcams. A 4:3 ratio is common on older devices; most platforms will pillarbox or stretch the image, which looks unprofessional. An unexpected ratio should prompt a device software update or a camera configuration adjustment.
  • Image sharpness: Use the still-capture feature to take a photo and inspect fine details. If the image appears soft, check whether your autofocus is functioning, whether the lens is dirty (clean camera lens), and whether lighting conditions are adequate.
  • Brightness and image clarity: A well-lit face is the single biggest factor in output excellence. Even a modest webcam produces professional results with good front lighting. A bright background or dimly lit room causes exposure issues that no amount of resolution can fix.

Testing Your Webcam for Zoom, Teams, and Google Meet — App-Specific Camera Access

After confirming that your webcam functions in the browser tester, validate it inside the conferencing application you actually use. Each platform has its own configuration panel where you can see a real-time preview and adjust defaults.

  • Zoom: Open the application → Settings → Video. Your webcam should appear in the camera dropdown. Use the Test Meeting feature — a private session that runs before the real one — to check your stream, lighting, and sound input together. Enable HD if your camera supports 1080p.
  • Microsoft Teams: Open the collaboration platform → Settings → Devices. Under Camera, select your device and watch the live preview. The platform also offers a Make a test call button that captures a short voice clip and plays it back, covering both picture and sound in one step.
  • Google Meet: Before joining, click the three dots → Settings → Video. Select your camera from the dropdown and observe the preview. The platform does not offer a standalone test call, so run this tester first as your pre-call check.
  • Skype: Open the messaging app → Settings → Audio & Video. Your feed should appear immediately. The panel also tests the integrated sound input and speaker simultaneously, making it a useful all-in-one communication check.

Pro Tip: Run the online webcam testing tool on this page before every important call. It takes under 30 seconds, catches permission resets that can occur after web client updates, and gives you the device details you need to resolve issues quickly. Think of it as your pre-call check routine — like checking your tie before walking into a boardroom.

Worked Example 1 — Remote Worker Preparing for a Video Call Interview: A remote worker opens this page the morning of a job interview conducted over a popular meeting platform. They click Start, allow camera access, and immediately see a 1080p feed at 30 fps in the camera preview. The Camera Information panel confirms: Webcam Resolution: 1920×1080, Frame Rate: 30 fps, Aspect Ratio: 16:9, Webcam Megapixels: 2.07 MP, and an integrated sound input detected. They take a still to check sharpness and lighting — the face is well-lit, centred, and sharp. Confident the configuration is solid, they open the meeting app, select the same device in the camera dropdown, and join the interview without a moment of technical anxiety. The 30-second investment pays off.

When Your Webcam Isn't Working: Troubleshoot Common Camera Problems

A failed webcam check almost always falls into one of three categories: the device not being detected, application software blocking the signal, or access rights preventing the web client from reaching the device. Working through these systematically saves time and avoids unnecessary replacements. Diagnosing issues is straightforward once you know which layer is failing.

Common Reasons a Camera Test Fails — Webcam Not Working Causes

If your camera is not responding after the tester runs, these are the most frequent causes:

  • Camera not connected — for external webcams, the connector cable may not be seated fully in the port. An LED on the device is often the quickest way to confirm power.
  • Broken cable or faulty cable — physical cable damage is a common device-side cause, particularly on cables that are frequently coiled, bent, or stepped on.
  • Device disabled — Windows and macOS both allow per-app or device-level camera disabling. A single toggle in Privacy & Security can block every app at once.
  • Camera blocked by web client access controls — after a client update or a site permission reset, the tester may show a black screen even though the hardware is fine. The fix is to re-grant access in the web client's site controls.
  • Camera used by another app — a meeting platform, a virtual camera driver, or other visual tools can hold an exclusive lock on the camera. Close other visual apps and conflicting programs before re-testing.
  • Outdated or missing device software — stale drivers in the driver stack cause flicker, black screens, and incorrect resolution reporting. This is especially common after a major OS update.
  • Unavailable camera — occasionally a process locking the camera at the OS level prevents any app from acquiring the stream. A device restart clears these locks instantly.
  • Webcam not detected — if the web client reports no camera devices, check whether the device appears in the hardware manager (Windows) or System Information (Mac). Absence there confirms an OS-level recognition failure.

Fixing Connection and Hardware Issues — Device Connections and USB Ports

Start with physical connections before touching any application setting. Device-side problems are fast to diagnose and eliminate:

  • Unplug the webcam from its current port and plug it into a different one. Some ports deliver less power or have compatibility restrictions — trying multiple ports rules this out.
  • Check that the connector is plugged in securely and properly connected at both ends. On cameras with detachable cables, reseat the connector at the camera body as well.
  • Confirm the camera is powered on — some external webcams have a physical power switch or require a powered hub.
  • If the status light remains off after trying multiple ports, test the camera on another computer to determine whether the fault is in the webcam or in the host machine.
  • A camera that fails on all computers is likely physically faulty or has a defective sensor, at which point it should be replaced or fixed rather than further diagnosed.
  • Clean the camera lens with a soft cloth if the feed is blurry — a dirty lens is a surprisingly common cause of poor image sharpness.

Worked Example 2 — Mac User Whose Camera Stopped Working: A Mac user opens this page and clicks the Start button. The camera preview area remains dark — no feed appears and the Camera Information panel shows no device. She opens the native camera utility; the same black screen. This rules out a web-client-only issue. She opens System Preferences → Security and Privacy → Camera and finds that her web client is unchecked — a recent OS update had reset the access rights. She ticks the entry, returns to this page, and clicks Refresh page. The live feed appears immediately. Total resolution time: 90 seconds. The issue was camera access disabled at the OS configuration level, not a device failure.

Resolving Software, Permission Conflicts, and Driver Problems

Once the physical component is confirmed good, application layers are the next target. These steps address the most common resolution approaches for software-caused failures:

  • Fix access rights at the OS level: On Windows, go to Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera and re-enable access for apps. On Mac, use System Preferences → Security and Privacy → Camera to enable access for each web client individually. These are your operating system's camera access controls.
  • Clear web client access rights: In the Chromium-based client, open Settings → Privacy and Security → Site Settings → Camera and remove any blocked entries. In the open-source web client, click the lock icon in the URL bar, select Connection Secure, and clear camera rights for this site. This resolves access-denied errors caused by previously blocked prompts.
  • Restart the web client: Closing and reopening the application flushes cached permission states and releases any resource locks held from a previous session.
  • Refresh device software: Open the hardware manager (Windows) or visit the manufacturer website (Mac/open-source OS) to install updated drivers. Stale device software is a primary cause of black screens and resolution degradation. Camera drivers are often bundled with broader chipset or controller updates.
  • Check for system conflicts: Clashes between virtual camera applications, broadcast tools, or meeting platforms can make a physical camera appear in-use to other programs. Uninstall or disable virtual tools temporarily to diagnose camera access issues.
  • Try an alternative web client — if the camera works in one browser but not another, the issue is in that client's access settings or site rights, not in the device or OS.
  • Use a quick check on a second device to confirm the camera is not defective before attempting a full driver reinstall.

Resolving Webcam Not Working Issues — When to Consider Upgrading

Some common webcam problems are symptoms of an ageing or faulty unit rather than a fixable configuration issue. Consider upgrading when:

  • The feed freezes randomly, flickers persistently, or produces consistent distortion even after driver reinstalls — signs of component failure.
  • Maximum resolution is stuck at 480p despite confirmed 1080p capability in the specifications — a sign of internal sensor degradation or outdated device support that no longer covers the unit.
  • The status light never illuminates despite confirmed power delivery — possible sign the camera is physically faulty.
  • You are moving into more demanding use cases — live broadcast on social platforms, high-stakes client meetings, or professional online presentations — where poor output creates a negative impression.

When evaluating new hardware, look at specifications including field of view (a 90-degree wide-angle suits group settings; narrower angles work better for solo one-on-one calls), autofocus performance, low-light sensitivity, and whether the unit is plug-and-play without requiring additional installation. Use this webcam tester after setup to immediately confirm the new device's image dimensions, capture rate, and colour reproduction before your next important call.

Worked Example 3 — Windows User Verifying Camera Before an Online Meeting: A Windows user wants to confirm his webcam is detected correctly before a company-wide collaboration platform call. He opens this page in his Chromium-based web client, clicks Start, clicks Allow when the access prompt appears, and sees his face in the camera preview within two seconds. The Camera Information panel shows: Frame Rate: 30 fps, Webcam Resolution: 1280×720, Aspect Ratio: 16:9, Webcam Megapixels: 0.92 MP, and an integrated sound input detected. He notes the 720p resolution — acceptable but not ideal — and decides to check the platform settings. In the collaboration tool → Settings → Devices, he selects the same webcam, enables HD output in the camera configuration panel, and refreshes the preview. The resolution upgrades to 1080p. The quick test and the settings check together took less than three minutes and ensured a polished, professional appearance for the call.

Frequently Asked Questions About the Webcam Test Online Tool

Which Devices Are Compatible and What Browsers Are Supported?

This webcam tester works on any device with a camera and a modern web client. Compatible devices include Windows laptops and desktops (including Microsoft Windows 11), Mac computers, open-source OS machines, Android phones, iPhones (running the Apple mobile browser), iPad tablets, and Chromebooks. Externally connected cameras are supported alongside built-in ones.

Supported clients include the Chromium-based browser, the open-source web client, the Apple browser (desktop and mobile), and Microsoft Edge. All four implement the getUserMedia API used for browser-based testing. On Android and other mobile clients, camera access works the same way as on desktop — the same grant-permission flow applies. If you encounter issues in one client, try an alternative to isolate whether the problem is application-specific. For users relying on assistive technology, accessibility is maintained across all supported clients.

Why Use a Free Online Webcam Tester Instead of Built-In Software?

Built-in OS tools like the Windows Camera app or the Mac's native camera utility confirm OS-level camera functionality, but they do not replicate how meeting platforms access your camera. A free webcam test run in the same web client you use for online meetings confirms that browser permission, device detection, capture rate, and sound input all work together as they will during a live call.

Additional advantages of using an online tool:

  • No application installation required — open the page, click Start, done. No downloads, no sign-up, no installation.
  • No downloads and no sign-up — the tool is available immediately, with single click access.
  • Cross-platform — the same page works on Windows, Mac, open-source OS environments, Android, and iPhone without configuration changes.
  • Reveals device details (resolution, capture rate, display ratio, sensor size, colour depth) that built-in OS apps do not surface.
  • Serves as a baseline confirmation for web-client-specific access states that the native camera utility cannot check.
  • Supports autostart on revisit, so your next quick check is even faster.

What Technical Camera Information Does the Tester Show?

The Camera Information panel displays everything surfaced by the web client's media API: the device label and model, real capture rate, active pixel dimensions, display ratio, calculated sensor size, camera orientation, integrated sound input status, speaker status, lossless still weight, compressed still weight, and a pixel-sampled colour count.

This data is surfaced from the live feed and processed locally in the web client — the detection routine runs client-side using an open-source JavaScript library. No data is sent to any external server; all processing is local. No footage is stored, no stills are saved — everything stays on your device. This is the definition of a browser-based, no-video-stored, no-video-shared architecture.

Is My Privacy Protected During a Camera Test?

Your privacy is important to us. This tool is built around a core principle: all our tests run on the client side — which means that we do not and can not see or record the image coming from your webcam. Your webcam footage never leaves your device. There is no capture, no upload, no storage, and no third-party access to your feed. The protection is architectural — technically impossible to bypass because the stream is consumed locally by your web client and never transmitted over a network.

This approach also means the tool is fully compliant with corporate IT policies that restrict external data transmission. Whether you are in a remote work environment, a school network, or a secure enterprise environment, you can run this private and secure check without any data concerns. Your camera access is used only to display the feed to you and to extract device details — nothing else. This is what no-upload, no-installation, and locally-processed means in practice.

What Should I Check If the Test Failed — Step-by-Step Solutions

If the FAQ section and the resolution steps above did not fix your issue, work through this final checklist:

  • Confirm the camera is plugged in securely and the connector cable is not damaged — a faulty cable is a top cause of intermittent failures.
  • Check that no other app has the camera locked — another program holding the resource prevents the web client from acquiring the stream. Close conflicting applications including meeting platforms and any virtual camera tool.
  • Ensure camera access is enabled in your OS data-protection settings — both at the device level and the per-app level.
  • Click refresh page to reset the permission request — sometimes a stale session holds an outdated access state.
  • Try the tool in an alternative web client — if it works in one browser but not another, the issue is in that client's access rights for this site, not in the device.
  • Restart the device to clear system conflicts and any process locking the camera at the OS level.
  • Install updated device software through the hardware manager or the manufacturer website to resolve stale or missing driver issues.
  • If all steps fail and the camera remains undetected across multiple computers, the webcam may be physically faulty and require professional repair or replacement. A defective unit that cannot be affordably repaired is best replaced with a modern plug-and-play model — choosing a webcam with current driver support and strong setup documentation eliminates most of these issues from the start.

This free online test webcam online tool is designed to be your first stop for diagnostics, your image-dimension reference, and your confidence check before every important call, capture session, or online appearance. Run it regularly — especially after OS updates — and your productivity, connectivity, and on-screen professional experience will stay consistently high.

faq.question: What is the difference between a camera test and a webcam test?
faq.answer: A webcam test checks whether your browser can access and display your camera feed — it's browser-based and ideal for verifying your setup before video calls. A camera test typically refers to a broader hardware-level check, which can include resolution, FPS, focus, and connectivity — often done through the OS or a dedicated app. The right choice depends on your device and use case.

faq.question: Which browsers support online webcam tests?
faq.answer: Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox offer the widest support for browser-based webcam testing, as they fully implement the WebRTC and MediaDevices APIs. Safari supports webcam access on macOS and iOS but may require explicit permission grants. Microsoft Edge also works well. Avoid outdated or niche browsers for best results.

faq.question: Why isn't my webcam being detected during an online test?
faq.answer: The most common reasons are: camera access blocked in browser permissions, outdated or missing device drivers, another app using the camera simultaneously, or a loose USB connection. Refresh the browser page and look for a permission prompt. If testing an external webcam, try a different USB port or cable.

faq.question: How do I test my webcam on Windows without a browser?
faq.answer: Open the built-in Camera app on Windows (search 'Camera' in the Start menu). If your webcam is detected and displaying a live feed, it's working at the hardware level. This rules out driver issues before moving to browser-based tests. For detailed info like FPS and resolution, use Device Manager or a tool like OBS Studio.

faq.question: How do I test my camera on Mac or Linux?
faq.answer: On macOS, open FaceTime or Photo Booth — if the live preview appears, your camera is functional. On Linux, use the 'Cheese' webcam application or run a browser-based test in Firefox or Chrome. You can also use the terminal command `ls /dev/video*` to confirm the device is recognised by the system.

faq.question: How can I check my webcam quality for professional video meetings?
faq.answer: During a browser-based test, look for a clear, sharp image without excessive noise or grain. Check that your frame rate appears smooth (ideally 30 FPS or higher), your lighting is even, and the camera auto-focuses quickly. For Zoom, Teams, or Google Meet, use the in-app video preview under Settings before your meeting to confirm everything looks good.

faq.question: Is an online camera test safe and private?
faq.answer: Reputable online webcam tests run entirely within your browser and do not upload or save your video feed to any server. Your camera stream stays local. Always check that the site uses HTTPS and review its privacy policy before granting camera access. You can revoke access at any time through your browser's permission settings.

faq.question: What should I check during a webcam test to ensure the best video call experience?
faq.answer: Verify your camera is detected and the preview is clear and stable. Check that the frame rate isn't choppy, your image isn't too dark or washed out, and there's no significant lag. Also confirm your microphone works in sync if you're using a webcam with a built-in mic. Test in the same lighting conditions you'll use during your actual call.
